We're looking for stories that centre Indigenous voices and leadership in innovation, where technology serves community sovereignty rather than replacing it. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we explore how Cariboo and BC Indigenous nations are using technology on their own terms — for language revitalization, land stewardship, cultural preservation, and self-determined governance. We're looking for stories that centre Indigenous voices and leadership in innovation, where technology serves community sovereignty rather than replacing it.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Participants drinking beverages sweetened with aspartame, acesulfame-K, or sucralose lost a similar amount of weight to those drinking water, while both groups also saw improvements in waist size, body composition, and several metabolic measures.

items.title: [Fast Company] From nearsightedness to self-harm: Meta-review looks at how digital media impacts young people’s health
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Digital media has become inescapable, and there’s still a lot we don’t know about its effects on young people’s physical and mental health.

But we do have enough evidence of its harms to warrant government action, say the authors of a series on “digital determinants of health” published today in The Lancet.

The three-paper series and related meta-review, which analyzed existing research that included data from 9 million people younger than 25, were authored by experts from 10 different countries.

What the evidence says about digital harms

The study found consistent associations between problematic digital media use—meaning addiction-like patterns of use, rather than screen time alone—and various health outcomes.

Obesity, nearsightedness, lower back pain, and cardiometabolic risk were linked to overall screen time across different age groups. 

Other findings differed by age. For children, higher overall screen time “was associated with poorer socio-emotional and cognitive development, increased anxiety and depression, and poorer sleep quality,” the review says. 

For adolescents, specific patterns of digital engagement were associated with “reduced quality of life, sleep problems, lower physical activity, non-suicidal self-injury, suicidal ideation, and substance use.”

Overall, the meta-review said, “more than three-quarters of the reported exposure-outcome associations were adverse,” though there was also evidence of beneficial digital media use, like children watching educational content with caregivers, and adolescents using active video games.

“These age-related differences emphasize that digital media use is not a uniform phenomenon,” the meta-review said. 

Roadblocks for research

Even with a large body of research to draw from, it’s difficult to quantify digital harms, and the authors stress that the available evidence doesn’t establish a cause-and-effect relationship between digital media use and specific health outcomes. 

Self-reported data has limitations, said Sunny Xun Liu, director of research at the Stanford Social Media Lab.

Liu, who was not involved in the Lancet series, coauthored a recent study in JAMA Pediatrics that looked at how often adolescents reported negative online experiences, finding that responses varied substantially depending on the platform. 

It can be hard to self-report media usage, Liu said. “If you ask [adolescents], ‘Okay, what type of harmful content have you seen in the past four weeks?’ it’s really hard for anybody to answer that question.”

Both Liu and the series authors said that better data does exist, but researchers often don’t have access to it.

“The most valuable data on how these platforms actually affect users are hidden within technology companies, limiting independent scrutiny and slowing scientific progress,” series author Louise Holly, a policy and research coordinator at the Digital Transformations for Health Lab in the U.K., said in a statement. 

One of the series’ key recommendations is that governments should require tech companies to share that data with vetted public-interest researchers.

A public health approach to digital media regulation

Even in the absence of that data, the series authors say the scale of the evidence of digital harms is great enough that we should take action now.

They approach the topic from a public health perspective, and call for more research and more regulation, noting that single measures—like app age limits—aren’t enough.

“Technology companies are borrowing a playbook well known from tobacco and fossil fuels: Manufacture doubt, discredit critics, frame regulation as a threat to freedom,” series author Barbara Prainsack, a political science professor at the University of Vienna in Austria, said in a statement. 

A public health approach that examines evidence across the whole population would counter that strategy, Prainsack said. 

“Seen that way, good regulation isn’t the enemy of innovation—it’s a driver of good innovation, channeling it toward safety and trust,” she said. “And when regulation is missing, it doesn’t mean that a technology is ungoverned; it just means that companies set the rules instead of public policy.”

Liu agreed that the public health approach is important, and suggested several considerations for researchers and policymakers, recommending they “really listen to young people,” think about how to better support overwhelmed family and caregivers, and, lastly, that researchers look for novel ways to conduct their studies and make the complexities of digital media use easier to understand.

items.title: [Fast Company] Meta’s new AI agent gave a stranger a user’s home address. Then he showed up
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Another day, another AI agent gone rogue.

Over the weekend, what seemed like a pretty typical Facebook Marketplace transaction took a very bizarre turn when Matt Robb, a Toronto-based tech video creator, let Muse handle his communications. Several hours later, Robb learned that, unbeknownst to him, Meta’s new AI agent had accepted a lowball offer for a keyboard and arranged a time for the buyer to come pick up the item—even though Robb wasn’t home at the time. 

“A guy just showed up at my door, ready to buy, because as far as he knew, we had a deal,” Robb wrote on Threads after learning of the mix-up from the AI agent. “Absolutely wild.”

While Robb later clarified that he had pre-authorized the agent to give out his address and accept offers, the mishap still exposed vulnerabilities in the system. In response, Robb sent feedback to David Singleton, who heads up the Meta Superintelligence Labs at the Menlo Park, California-based company. Robb even patched things up with the buyer, Usman Naseem, who was understandably disgruntled to arrive at Robb’s apartment ready to buy a keyboard only to be ghosted once there. Naseem posted on Threads that Robb delivered the keyboard along with some valuable items as a gift. 

Still, the whole ordeal serves as a cautionary tale of sorts.

WHAT WENT WRONG

It seems that some of the settings were to blame for how this transaction went off the rails.

Robb noted that when allowing Muse to handle his Facebook Marketplace interactions, he had selected the “allow always” option in lieu of “allow one time.” Robb said that he thought that the AI agent would send approvals to accept offers, which it didn’t do. “Be careful,” he cautioned others.

As Robb posted, granting Muse permission to send messages on his behalf explains why his address was provided during the communications with Naseem. “I didn’t think it would send it out to everyone that gave me an offer, so it’s worth checking,” he wrote on Threads. 

Indeed, Robb only learned about Naseem coming to his home when Muse later informed him with a string of messages that read, in part, “I should probably stop the auto-replies from claiming you’re home when I can’t verify that.” 

What’s more, even after Robb instructed Muse to stop giving out his address, he decided to test it by asking a few friends to see if the AI agent would still share this information. The bot provided his address to five more people.

As for the lowball offer that was accepted, Robb wrote that the Meta team he met with told him that occurred because of an internal error. 

Based on his experience, Robb also said that he suggested an improvement to Meta. Specifically, he recommended that any messages sent by Muse include a note underneath the message so that everyone in the conversation knows that. “We definitely need clearer signals when an AI is talking on someone’s behalf (it should have a ‘Sent by Muse’ tag), and much tighter restrictions on sensitive info,” he posted.

AI “GETTING INTRUSIVE”

Muse is only the latest instance of an AI tool going rogue. There’s now a growing list of problematic cases of various AI tools—including the hacking of a startup by two OpenAI models and the troubling messages between a Florida man and Google’s Gemini tool before he ultimately committed suicide.

In the week following Meta’s release of Muse, it’s been downloaded 3 million times, according to The Guardian. But the mess-up only provides more fodder for people who already have concerns about AI agents, particularly in the wake of several doomsday warnings from AI leaders earlier this month. 

While Robb was patient zero for Muse’s first major mess-up, he said that he was “glad” that it happened to him instead of someone who might be more vulnerable. “I’m just saying the average user will prompt worse than a tech guy.” 

And even though he noted that his experience may have illustrated how AI is “getting intrusive,” Robb said he’s not dissuaded from the technology. “I’m not an anti-AI person at all,” he wrote.

items.title: [Fast Company] Grindr is spending $250M to signal that it’s getting serious about LGBTQ+ healthcare
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Grindr is expanding its footprint in LGBTQ-focused healthcare with its first major acquisition. The dating app is paying $250 million for health startup Freddie, with the aim of fully integrating Freddie’s HIV-prevention telehealth and pharmacy capabilities into a broader Grindr Health offering.

The launch of Grindr Health builds on the company’s telehealth business Woodwork, which launched in 2025 to connect users with medication for weight loss and erectile dysfunction. As of Wednesday, when the acquisition was announced, users can access features from both Freddie and Woodwork through a Grindr Health portal in the app.

Grindr CEO George Arison has long credited the app with helping to make HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) more mainstream. The preventive medication is 99% effective at reducing the sexual transmission of the virus.

As of 2025, the United States reached a record high of more than 644,000 PrEP users, a 10% increase from 2024. But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that 2.2 million Americans could benefit from PrEP—meaning the medicine is still reaching less than a third of its potential users in the country, and there’s a lot of room for Grindr’s new business to grow.

“It’s a situation where everybody that can be on this drug should be on this drug, because it’s healthier for them and healthier for people that they meet,” Arison tells Fast Company. “To us, [PrEP access] seems like a natural opportunity and a win-win, to both build a great business as well as do something really important for public health,” he says.

Adding a pharmacy to the gayborhood

Arison says contracting HIV is “the one thing that all gay men are scared of,” suggesting that taking PrEP should be common sense for the app’s users. But mirroring broader U.S. statistics, Grindr reports that only 400,000 of its millions of American users identify as being on PrEP.

“If we achieve the same market share in the U.S. on PrEP that Freddie has in Canada . . . that will mean [an additional] 200,000 people on PrEP, and that will mean about 5,000 people not getting HIV a year,” Arison adds. With the most recent CDC findings showing an estimated 31,800 new HIV infections in the U.S. per year, that means Grindr could play a significant role in driving down HIV infections nationwide.

Adding in more healthcare to complement Woodwork—which initially offered erectile dysfuynction medication and has since expanded to include GLP-1s—is part of Arison’s effort to make users (and investors) see Grindr as a “global gayborhood,” not just a place for hookups. The company has been leveraging AI to build new features that improve the user experience and offer specific insights about people that users might want to connect with.

“Don’t think of Grindr as a dating product. Think of Grindr as a social network that has a very unique pulse on the user base,” he says. “Obviously, we needed to prove to everyone that that’s what we were. This is just a logical next step in that direction.”

Good for health, good for business

As Arison has been expanding his vision for Grindr beyond just connecting people, he’s also been improving the company’s revenue and subscriber base.

In the second quarter of 2026, Grindr reported a revenue of $138 million, a 33% year-over-year increase. Meanwhile, the app’s paying user base continues to grow, with a current 1.4 million users paying for Grindr features including its XTRA and Unlimited subscription tiers, up 16% from last year.

Researchers at Morgan Stanley noted the clear rationale for Grindr’s acquisition of Freddie, pointing to the app’s earlier telehealth success through Woodwork. And even before that launch, Grindr successfully connected more than 2 million users with mpox vaccines in 2022.

The analysts also highlighted Freddie’s strong earning potential for Grindr. The telehealth platform has higher gross margins than its peers, as Freddie generates revenue from referral fees to entities receiving federal discounts through the U.S.’s 340B Drug Pricing Program.

With each active patient estimated to generate $4,800 in revenue for a full year, Arison sees the acquisition as a financial no-brainer as well. If the company achieves it’s baseline goal of 50,000 Grindr users getting PrEP through the app, it would generate $240 million in revenue annually.

Moving forward, Arison says the acquisition sets the brand up “for a much broader Grindr Health vision.” One example? Putting users in touch with health professionals who are part of or experts on LGTBQ+ health.

“I talk to so many people—myself included, honestly—who want a gay doctor and cannot get a gay doctor,” Arison says. “Over time, we can be in a place where we’re giving way more capability to our users to find gay doctors, and be able to connect with them virtually for their other healthcare needs.”

The dating app is paying $250 million for health startup Freddie , with the aim of fully integrating Freddie’s HIV-prevention telehealth and pharmacy capabilities into a broader Grindr Health offering.
